articles.title: A Toy Company, AI, and the Human Argument
articles.excerpt: If anyone can make it, no one can sell it. This month, the people who make Dungeons & Dragons and Magic: The Gathering moved to unionize. Most of the coverage is about pay, crunch, and layoffs, and th…
articles.body: If anyone can make it, no one can sell it. This month, the people who make Dungeons & Dragons and Magic: The Gathering moved to unionize. Most of the coverage is about pay, crunch, and layoffs, and those are real. But buried in the D&D team's letter is the sentence that explains the last three years at Wizards of the Coast: "As pressure has ramped up from Hasbro to adopt LLMs and Gen AI tools in various aspects of our work, WOTC has resisted these efforts and kept AI out of our games. That's good! We want to preserve this commendable stance through a union contract that ensures our games will always be made by people for people." Read that again. The workers are not asking the company to adopt a policy. The policy already exists.

articles.title: Why my STL to CAD script was 8 mm off on a printer part, and the fix
articles.excerpt: mesh2cad turns an STL into CAD. Every part gets a STEP file with real planes, cylinders and cones. When the part is simple enough it also gets a CadQuery or OpenSCAD script with named parameters, so y…
articles.body: mesh2cad turns an STL into CAD. Every part gets a STEP file with real planes, cylinders and cones. When the part is simple enough it also gets a CadQuery or OpenSCAD script with named parameters, so you can change hole_3_d instead of editing triangles. I test on six real Original Prusa i3 MK3S parts. After the last post all six were exact STEP, but only three had a script. 0.13.0 adds a fourth: y-motor-holder. What was wrong Last time I wrote that y-motor-holder was refused because its screw holes are stepped and don't go through the part. That was true, but it wasn't the main problem. The script vocabulary built a solid by taking the outline of the part seen along X, Y and Z, extruding each one the full length of the part, and intersecting them.

articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady What I Built I built LazyNotes AI, a lightweight Python tool powered by an open-weight model that automatically reads messy, unorganized notes, meeting logs, or raw text dumps and condenses them into clear summaries. Between managing daily tasks, exam prep, and constant notifications, I constantly catch myself putting off reading long logs or sorting through unstructured quick notes. LazyNotes channels inner "sloth energy" by automating that tedious reading process so I can stay lazy while my local machine handles the heavy lifting in the background.

articles.title: There Is No Unstructured Data
articles.excerpt: Pick up a supplier contract. It is a PDF, forty pages, scanned at a slight angle. In ten seconds you know who the parties are, when it starts, when it can be cancelled, what the penalty is for late de…
articles.body: Pick up a supplier contract. It is a PDF, forty pages, scanned at a slight angle. In ten seconds you know who the parties are, when it starts, when it can be cancelled, what the penalty is for late delivery and which law applies. You see a header, a list of obligations, a table of prices and two signatures. Now ask your data platform what it sees. It sees a blob. Content type application/pdf , size 2.3 MB, last modified Tuesday. In the catalog, if it is in a catalog at all, it is filed under one word: unstructured. So which one of you is unstructured? We built an industry around a limitation For fifty years the rule of data has been simple: structure first, then ask. Before a question can be answered, someone has to turn the world into rows and columns.

articles.title: TurtleShell: Let a Local Tortoise Turn Messy Git History into Standups
articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady Standup time has a familiar ritual: open the terminal, scan a handful of commits called wip, it works now, a…
articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady What I Built Standup time has a familiar ritual: open the terminal, scan a handful of commits called wip , it works now , and fix typo , then try to remember what the work actually meant. I built TurtleShell 🐢 , a local-first tool that inspects a Git repository and turns recent commit messages and filtered diff excerpts into two useful drafts: A standup with Yesterday , Today , and Blockers sections. A changelog grouped into Features , Fixes , and Chores . The dashboard also compares raw commits with the generated summary and lets me copy the standup to Slack. When MongoDB Atlas is configured, TurtleShell saves generated updates for later search.

articles.title: What actually triggers Claude's 5-hour limit (and the four ways around it)
articles.excerpt: If you have hit "You've reached your usage limit. You can resume in X hours" in the middle of a refactor, the useful question is not how many messages you get. It is what the clock is measuring and wh…
articles.body: If you have hit "You've reached your usage limit. You can resume in X hours" in the middle of a refactor, the useful question is not how many messages you get. It is what the clock is measuring and when it started. The window is rolling, not daily The five-hour limit is a rolling window. The timer starts at the timestamp of your first message in a usage session , not at midnight and not at the moment you get blocked. Two consequences follow, and they explain most of the confusion: Two people on identical plans hit their limits at completely different clock times. The five hours you wait is measured from when you started , so a burst that begins at 09:00 unlocks at 14:00 even if you hit the wall at 09:40.

articles.title: SlothSort — Tidy Files, Slowly
articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady My Downloads folder has a familiar problem: files accumulate faster than I organize them. Screenshots end up…
articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady What I Built My Downloads folder has a familiar problem: files accumulate faster than I organize them. Screenshots end up beside lecture notes, code files get buried under documents, and filenames like document1.pdf, IMG_1234.jpg, and final_final_v2.txt don't make finding anything easier. I built SlothSort, a local-first, AI-powered file organizer that does the tedious part for me. SlothSort scans a selected directory, including nested folders, and suggests categories and more descriptive filenames using an open-weight Qwen model running locally through Ollama. It also detects exact duplicate files using SHA-256 hashing.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 25, 1671: Astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovers Iapetus, Saturn's 'yin-yang' moon
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 25, 1671, the Italian astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovered a new moon at Saturn! Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 25, 1671, the Italian astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovered a new moon at Saturn! Iapetus was the second moon anyone had ever found orbiting Saturn, and it was the first of four moons Cassini would discover at the ringed planet. The Dutch astronomer Christiaan Huygens had discovered Titan , the largest of Saturn's moons, about six years earlier. After Cassini found Iapetus, he also found the moons Rhea, Tethys and Dione. When Cassini first saw Iapetus, the moon looked like a tiny speck on the west side of Saturn. He calculated its orbit and thought he would be able to see it again on the east side of Saturn 39 days later, but it was nowhere to be seen.

articles.title: Pennsylvania will require labels on AI-generated ads
articles.excerpt: On Thursday, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro signed the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act into law, requiring disclosures on AI-generated ads. The law requires any ad - whether it's…
articles.body: On Thursday, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro signed the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act into law, requiring disclosures on AI-generated ads. The law requires any ad - whether it's a still image, video, audio, or text - that "has been significantly modified or generated by artificial intelligence" to include a label in the same format as the ad itself. That applies to TV commercials from multi-billion-dollar companies , as well as restaurants' ugly, crowded flyers about their wing specials. articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 24, 1946: V-2 rocket takes 1st photos of Earth from space
articles.excerpt: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. While these grainy, black-and-white images might not look like much today, they were a huge deal at the time, because no one had ever seen Earth from space before. The V-2 rocket launched from the White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico. It carried a 35-millimeter motion picture camera that captured a new frame every second and a half. The rocket soared to an altitude of about 65 miles before falling back to Earth. Both the rocket and the camera were destroyed after crashing into the Earth at a speed of about 340 miles per hour. But the film survived because it was protected inside a steel case. Scientists had to drive out into the New Mexico desert to retrieve the film.

articles.title: 'Star Trek: Strange New Worlds' was afraid to say anything in season of gimmicks
articles.excerpt: The fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was one giant gimmick: shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres.
articles.body: It didn’t take long for fans to figure out that the fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was going to be unlike any season of " Star Trek " before it. The entire season was one giant gimmick, and that gimmick was shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres. You could argue that an entire season of gimmick episodes is a bold risk: putting the characters in fun, wacky situations to see how they react. It could be interesting, but the season we got never made the most of the concept. It was all so safe and paint-by-numbers, and, most importantly, it didn't have anything profound or interesting to say. That should trouble any Trekkie.
